summary: Looks at the benefits and problems of allowing RTCP packets to be smaller by relaxing the compound packet rules in RFC 3550. Based on that analysis, it defines certain changes to those rules for sessions that agree to use them.

plainLanguage.summary: In an RTP call, control messages normally travel inside a large bundle that always includes a status report and a name tag. RFC 5506 lets a session agree to send urgent feedback as a small packet on its own, which saves space and delay. The trade-off is that some older equipment may throw the small packets away.

questions: can rtcp packets be sent without compound packets
when can rtcp skip the compound packet rules
does reduced-size rtcp work with srtp
how big is a compound rtcp packet
subtitle: Letting RTP feedback travel as small RTCP packets instead of the full compound bundle.

tldr.problem: RFC 3550 requires every RTCP packet to be a compound packet holding at least a sender or receiver report and a CNAME item, so even a tiny feedback message travels in a large bundle that can be delayed or dropped on slow links.
tldr.mechanism: For sessions using the AVPF or SAVPF profile, RFC 5506 allows extra feedback to be sent as Reduced-Size RTCP, signalled with the SDP attribute a=rtcp-rsize, while scheduled reports stay compound.
tldr.outcome: Feedback such as a NACK or a codec control request can be sent quickly and cheaply. The catch is that old receivers and middle boxes may discard the smaller packets, so senders must check that they arrive.

today: RFC 5506 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it updates RFC 3550, RFC 3711 and RFC 4585, so it is the definition of Reduced-Size RTCP and the a=rtcp-rsize attribute.

sections.title: Why the Compound Rule Is a Problem
sections.content:
In RTP, RFC 3550 makes it mandatory to send RTCP as compound packets: a sender report (SR) or receiver report (RR), followed by a source description (SDES) packet carrying at least the CNAME item. That makes the smallest RTCP packet quite large.

The RTP/AVPF profile (RFC 4585) adds feedback messages that benefit from being sent with minimal delay. On low-bitrate links these messages can consume many resources and add delay while the whole bundle is sent. RFC 5506 therefore proposes sending just the feedback, as Reduced-Size RTCP.

The document updates RFC 3550, RFC 3711 and RFC 4585.
sections.plainLanguage: Every small control message must be sent inside a bigger bundle. On a slow link the bundle takes time to travel, so a quick note inside it arrives too late to be useful.

sections.title: What Compound Packets Provide
sections.content:
Before relaxing the rule, the RFC lists why compound packets exist. Sender and receiver reports tell every participant which SSRCs are in the session, so everyone can estimate the group size, which the RTCP transmission scheduling relies on. Failing to do so could make RTCP senders consume too much bandwidth. The reports also carry basic statistics used for monitoring and adaptation.

The CNAME item lets receivers decide which media flows should be synchronized, and sender reports carry the NTP and RTP timestamps used to do that. The CNAME is also the longer identifier used to tell an SSRC collision from an RTP-level routing loop.

The RFC concludes that both the SR/RR and the CNAME are very important, especially for new participants, and that their value drops if they are not sent regularly.
sections.plainLanguage: The bundle carries a head count, a name tag and a clock check. Newcomers depend on those, so the bundle still has to be sent at regular intervals.

sections.title: Use Cases and Benefits
sections.content:
The RFC names four use cases: control plane signalling (the Open Mobile Alliance Push-to-talk over Cellular service), codec control such as TMMBR messages from RFC 5104, feedback such as generic NACK for video, and small status reports that could even be sent unencrypted for network monitoring.

The saving is concrete. An RR with a report block for one source is 32 bytes and an SR is 52 bytes. The SDES packet with a CNAME is 10 bytes plus the CNAME string length. A Reduced-Size RTCP packet can therefore be at least 70-80 bytes smaller than a compound packet.

Smaller packets are less likely to be dropped on links where loss grows with packet size, such as radio links, and they take less time to serialize. The RFC's example is that 120 bytes over a 30 kbps link takes 32 milliseconds. Smaller feedback also keeps RTCP bandwidth lower during heavy feedback periods.
sections.plainLanguage: A short note is less likely to be lost on a poor connection and gets through faster than a thick bundle. That matters most for urgent feedback on slow links.

sections.title: Known Issues
sections.content:
Middle boxes may discard RTCP that does not follow the compound rules, or treat an unfamiliar packet type as unknown, so a compound packet might get through while a Reduced-Size one is lost.

The packet validation code in Appendix A of RFC 3550 would discard Reduced-Size RTCP. Updated code must accept a first packet that is not an SR or RR, which weakens validation. Old receivers would drop the small packets entirely, which can split a session into old receivers that see only compound feedback and newer ones that see both, and it can skew the avg_rtcp_size calculation.

SRTP (RFC 3711) states that the first part of an SRTCP packet must be an SR or RR, but the RFC finds SRTP has no real dependency on that, so Reduced-Size RTCP can be used with it, though SRTP implementations MAY need changes. Multiplexing RTP and RTCP on one port and header compression raise further points left partly to future work.
sections.plainLanguage: Some older equipment throws away anything that is not a full bundle. So before relying on small packets, a sender has to check that they actually arrive at the other side.

sections.title: When Reduced-Size RTCP Is Allowed
sections.content:
Regular compound RTCP MUST keep being sent throughout the session, so group size tracking and synchronization still work and newcomers can learn about the senders. Reduced-Size RTCP SHOULD be limited to extra RTCP, such as feedback, sent when a regular compound packet would not otherwise have been sent.

It SHALL only be used in sessions running AVPF (RFC 4585) or SAVPF (RFC 5124) in Early RTCP or Immediate Feedback mode, and SHALL NOT be sent until at least one compound RTCP has been sent. In Immediate Feedback mode all feedback MAY be Reduced-Size. In Early RTCP mode, feedback scheduled as Early RTCP MAY be, but anything scheduled as Regular RTCP SHALL be compound.

A Reduced-Size RTCP packet holds one or more RTCP packets of any type, MUST NOT be used for regular scheduled reports, and MUST NOT be used with the RTP/AVP or RTP/SAVP profiles.
sections.plainLanguage: Small packets are only for urgent notes. The full bundle must still go out on schedule, and small packets may only be used after at least one full bundle has been sent.

sections.title: Verifying Delivery
sections.content:
Because packets may be dropped by old endpoints or middle boxes, any application using Reduced-Size RTCP MUST use an algorithm to detect consistent failure to deliver. The details are application dependent and outside the scope of the RFC.

Where delivery can be detected, it is easy to check. A sender report is confirmed by the echoed timestamp in a later receiver report. Many feedback messages show up as an effect, such as an RTP retransmission (RFC 4588) after a NACK, or a TMMBN after a TMMBR. Packet types whose delivery cannot be detected SHOULD NOT be sent as Reduced-Size RTCP unless they share a lower-layer datagram with a type that can be.

If verification fails, it is strongly RECOMMENDED to fall back to compound RTCP only. For size-sensitive links, sending a single RTCP packet per lower-layer datagram is strongly RECOMMENDED, and large Reduced-Size packets should just be sent as compound ones.
sections.plainLanguage: After sending a small note, look for a sign that it arrived, such as the reply it asks for. If no signs come, go back to sending the full bundle.

sections.title: Signalling With SDP
sections.content:
The RFC defines the a=rtcp-rsize Session Description Protocol (RFC 4566) attribute to show that a participant can support Reduced-Size RTCP. A participant that proposes its use must itself support receiving it.

An offering client that wishes to use it MUST include a=rtcp-rsize in the SDP offer, and an answerer that supports and wishes to use it SHALL include the attribute in the answer. In declarative uses of SDP, such as RTSP (RFC 2326) or the Session Announcement Protocol (RFC 2974), the presence of the attribute means the participant MAY use Reduced-Size RTCP.

IANA registered rtcp-rsize as a media-level property attribute that takes no value.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides say that they can read small packets before either sends one. Until both agree, everyone keeps using the full bundle.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RTP (RFC 3550) and AVPF (RFC 4585) also apply to Reduced-Size RTCP.

The weaker validation of received packets on the RTCP port may lead to spurious data being accepted as real RTCP. This can mostly be addressed by any security mechanism that provides authentication, one of which is SRTP (RFC 3711).
sections.plainLanguage: With looser checking at the door, fake packets could be mistaken for real control messages. A security mechanism that proves who sent a packet, such as SRTP, keeps them out.
